description: GEO ORYX is a student team with a background in Geomatics and skills in GIS, spatial analysis, coding, software development, design, and presentations. For Challenge 6, we aim to turn SAR imagery into clear maps and useful insights using SNAP, QGIS, and ArcGIS Pro. We value teamwork and practical learning, and welcome complementary skills in remote sensing, Python, and web development.
summary: MARSAD ("observatory" in Arabic) turns NISAR radar into a story anyone can read. Pick a place, drag a handle between two radar dates, play the time series and hear it, then read why the land changed or why it did not. Six prepared places on four continents show different rhythms: the seasonal pulse of water on the Indus plain, a solar park in Oman that changed with nothing new built, crop fields in Italy, a green monsoon the radar barely sees, the edge of the Amazon forest and a Greenland glacier. Every place can be seen in radar, in real colour and next to Sentinel-1 C-band. Visitors can also click any spot on Earth to ask NASA's catalogue what NISAR recorded there and run a live comparison. The explanation adapts to five audiences, and one report gathers them all. Radar data is free but hard to read; MARSAD makes it readable, and honest about what radar can and cannot tell.
details:
What it does

MARSAD is an open, interactive web app built on NISAR L-band radar (NASA and ISRO).

• Compare. A handle wipes between two NISAR dates on an interactive map.

• Track. A time slider plays every available date (9 to 17 per place) with a chart of what the radar measured. With sound on, each date plays a note: the rhythm of the land becomes audible.

• Understand the radar. One switch between the HH and HV channels, each with a plain sentence. Two rules open the site: rough surfaces shine, wet surfaces shine, calm water stays dark.

• See it three ways. NISAR radar, a real-colour picture (NASA HLS) and Sentinel-1 C-band (NASA OPERA RTC-S1) for the same weeks, side by side.

• Ask why, and why not. Each place has three cards: why it changed, why it did not, and what to read with care.

• Read any point. Click a point on the picture to get its radar brightness over time.

• Go anywhere. Click any place on Earth: MARSAD asks NASA's Common Metadata Repository, live, how many NISAR passes exist there, on which dates and with which channels. A small server then compares the first and latest NISAR picture of a 10 km square around the point (experimental).

• Five audiences, one report. "I am..." rewrites the explanation for the public, decision-makers, resource managers, educators and scientists. A full report with all five can be read on the site or saved as a PDF.

The six places and what we found

1. Sindh, Pakistan (the pulse of water). Dark, smooth surfaces grew from 164 km² (17 June 2026) to 309 km² (16 August) and fell to 90 km² (15 October). We checked this against NASA's optical water map (OPERA DSWx-HLS) on 12 dates. Where that map shows open water, the radar is dark in 55 to 99% of cells, so the rule holds. But only 6 to 80% of the dark area is confirmed as water, so the site calls it "dark, smooth surface" and not a measured flood extent.

2. Manah, Oman (the panels that danced). One of Oman's largest solar fields became 3.6 times brighter (+5.5 dB) between 4 and 16 September 2026, in the evening pass only. Optical pictures show nothing new was built, the dawn pass shows no change, and the field next to it stays flat. The jump falls when the sun at pass time drops from 6.4° to 9.1° below the horizon. The likely cause is the night position of sun-tracking panels. We first read it as new construction; the site tells that story as a lesson: radar shows that something changed, not what changed.

3. Po valley, Italy (the rhythm of the fields). Field by field, crops change the radar brightness through the season while the towns stay fixed.

4. Salalah, Oman (the green the radar cannot see). The khareef monsoon turns the mountains green, yet L-band brightness moves by less than 1.5 dB: the 24 cm wave passes through grass.

5. Rondônia, Brazil (where the forest ends). HV separates forest from pasture through cloud. About half of the window reads as forest (47 to 62% depending on the date). That swing is weather, not forest: wet pasture brightens. We do not claim new deforestation.

6. Jakobshavn, Greenland (ice that never stands still). By tracking the crevasse pattern between passes 12 days apart, we measured the ice moving 15 to 30 metres per day in the fast lane, towards the sea, while 73% of the tracked patches (rock and slow ice) did not move. Only HH exists there, and the very fastest ice could not be matched.

How it addresses the challenge

The challenge asks for a tool that tracks and visualises surface change with SAR at different time steps, explains the physical drivers of what we see or do not see, and speaks to the public, decision-makers, resource managers, educators and scientists. MARSAD does each of these with NISAR as its core data, and it treats "what we do not see" as seriously as what we do.

We also checked ourselves: the Sindh series mixes product versions, so we followed buildings that never change. Their brightness differs by 0.07 dB between the 2025 and 2026 products.

How we built it

A static site (React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS) on GitHub Pages. Python scripts read only the needed window from each multi-gigabyte NISAR GCOV file over HTTPS (h5py, fsspec), average the backscatter in linear power, re-project it and write small pictures and JSON files. Every number on the site is computed by these scripts from the data; none is typed by hand. The optional live analysis is a small FastAPI program reached through a tunnel.

Benefits

• Free NASA radar becomes readable without radar training: drag, play, listen, read why.

• It works in cloud, dust and night, when cameras cannot see.

• It is honest about limits: every place says what the radar cannot tell, and Manah shows how a change can be misread.

• Anyone can look at their own place and keep a report for others.

Tools and languages

JavaScript (React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS) for the site; Python (NumPy, h5py, fsspec, pyproj, Pillow, FastAPI) for processing and the live analysis; GitHub and GitHub Pages for code and hosting; Microsoft Dev Tunnels for the live-analysis server; Canva for the MARSAD logos. An SI coding assistant was used, as described in the SI field and in the README.

How is it creative?

• The challenge's own image, the dance and rhythm of the land, runs through the whole site: an opening built from our logo, a radar echo that turns into a landscape, and a sound mode where each date plays a note so the rhythm can be heard.

• It treats "what the radar does not see" as a result, not a failure: Salalah's green monsoon that L-band barely notices, and Manah, where a change we first read as new construction turned out to be an existing solar field, most likely its panels turning.

• Every place can be seen three ways (radar, real colour, C-band), and the explanation rewrites itself for five kinds of reader.

What factors did the team consider?

• Honesty: every number is computed from the data, each place has a "read with care" card, and we checked ourselves against second sources (NASA's optical water map for Sindh, optical pictures and a second orbit for Manah, rock that must not move for the Greenland ice speed, unchanging buildings for the mix of NISAR product versions).

• Access: a static site with no login, readable on a phone, and a report that can be saved as a PDF.

• What NISAR could give in its first months: dates from late 2025 to November 2026, so we chose places where change happens within a season.

• Rules: no NASA branding, SI use disclosed, no person under 18 in any material.

What is next (what we hope to achieve)

More years of NISAR will separate a normal season from an unusual one. Next steps: interferometry for ground motion, calibrated C-band numbers, tracking of the fastest ice, and alerts when a place leaves its usual rhythm.
